title: Maya, the passing pull
hook: the pull of the passing world, attractive and fleeting, is called maya

segments.voice: Yesterday, the five virtues: truth, contentment, compassion, humility and love. Your line was five guards at the door. Which guard stood up for you? Today, the pull those guards are guarding against. Day two hundred forty-one.
screen: `THE FIVE VIRTUES — FIVE GUARDS AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: You open your phone to check the weather. Forty minutes later you're watching a stranger restore a rusty knife, and you've added a jacket to a cart. Nothing bad happened. Everything was pretty. The knife was shiny, the jacket was soft, the video was calming. And none of it is what you meant to do with those forty minutes. Everybody knows this pull: bright, sweet, and gone the moment you look away. The Gurus had a word for it, long before phones. Today it's maya.
screen: `CHECK THE WEATHER.` → `FORTY MINUTES LATER.` → `ALL OF IT PRETTY.` → `MAYA.`

segments.voice: Maya is an old Indian word, and different traditions use it differently. In some Hindu schools it can mean the world as a kind of illusion. In the Guru Granth Sahib, the stress falls somewhere else. The world is real; the Creator made it and lives in it. Maya is the pull of the passing parts of it: money, status, comfort, attachment, anything bright that promises to last and doesn't. The problem isn't that things are fake. It's that we lean our whole weight on things that were only ever passing through. The Granth gives maya many pictures. Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru, has a short salok near the very end of the book. As a bubble rises on water and vanishes, he says, so the world is made; Nanak says, listen, friend. The bubble is real. It even has a rainbow on it. It just isn't a place to live. Other hymns call maya a snake wrapped around the world, or a shade that moves as the sun moves, so you can never sit in it for long. And notice what Sikh teaching does not say. It doesn't say run to the forest, give up your job, leave your family. The Gurus were householders. The ideal is to live in the middle of the bright, busy world and not be owned by it, like a lotus that grows in water and stays dry. That's the question maya asks on an ordinary afternoon: am I using this, or is it using me? Pretty isn't the enemy. Forgetting that it's passing is.
screen: `AN OLD WORD, USED MANY WAYS.` · `NOT FAKE — JUST PASSING.` · `A BUBBLE ON WATER.` · `IN THE WORLD, NOT OWNED BY IT.` · then, large: `PRETTY, AND PASSING.`

segments.voice: Think of one pull that got you today: a screen, a purchase, a worry about how you look, a craving. Don't scold yourself for it. Just picture it clearly, the way it shines. Now picture it as a bubble on water, catching the light. Say to yourself, quietly: pretty, and passing. Then let your attention come back to the breath, which is also passing, and also here. Stay with it. The bell holds the time.
Maya. In the Guru Granth Sahib, the pull of the passing world: bright, attractive, and gone. Not a lie, just not a home.
Your line: pretty, and passing. Today, when something pulls at you, pause for one breath before you follow it, and name it: pretty, and passing. Day two hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: Sikhs speak of maya as the pull of wealth, status and attachment; the Gurus taught living as householders in the world, working and raising families, while remembering the Name so as not to be ruled by that pull.

fork.setup: you want to be free of maya's pull. what does Sikh teaching point you toward?
options: leave home and live alone in the forest.
live in the busy world, working and caring, without being owned by it.
decide the world is an illusion and ignore it.
fork.reveal: the Gurus were householders. like a lotus in water, the ideal is to stay in the world and not be ruled by its passing pull.

original.note: Gurmukhi: maya, the pull of the passing world; in Gurbani it's often spelled and sung with three syllables.

trapdoor: what you thought: maya means everything is an illusion.
what it means: in Sikh teaching, the world is real, and maya is the pull of its passing things when we lean on them as if they lasted.

what a scholar hears: an old Sanskrit word with different meanings across Indian schools; the Granth often pictures it through images like a bubble, a snake and a moving shade, and pairs it with attachment (moh).

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1427 (Salok Mahala 9: the bubble on water)
Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 938 (Sidh Gosht: the lotus in water, living detached)

notes: The bubble salok (jaise jal te budbudaa upjai binsai neet) is cited to Ang 1427, Salok Mahala 9; confirm the Ang and salok number.

The lotus-in-water image is cited to Sidh Gosht (Ang 938); confirm the Ang.
